reading.title: The Extra Lunches
reading.text: At noon, the school kitchen had twelve extra lunches. The order sheet listed forty children, and the cook had prepared exactly forty meals. Only twenty-eight children were sitting in the dining room. The assistant first thought the missing group must be on a trip. However, the calendar showed no trip for that day. Then a teacher arrived carrying twelve empty trays. Her class was eating in the garden as part of a lesson about food waste. The lunches could not be unwanted: the class had specifically ordered them that morning. The assistant laughed at his own quick conclusion. Could the location of a meal matter as much as the number of meals? In this case, it did. He added a location column to the daily sheet. Counting carefully had not been enough; the team also needed to know where the children were. A full kitchen can still have an information gap.

questions.prompt: How many children were in the dining room? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Only twenty-eight children” — yigirma sakkiz.

questions.prompt: Where was the other class eating? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Her class was eating in the garden” — bog‘da.

questions.prompt: What column did the assistant add? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Added a location column” — joy ustuni.

listening.title: The Wrong Building
listening.text:
Nadia: Could this be the training centre? The number is right, but the sign says Dental Laboratory.
Peter: It can't be our centre. The invitation describes a building with a glass entrance, and this door is wooden.
Nadia: We must be on the wrong street. There are two streets with almost the same name: College Road and College Lane.
Peter: You're right. Our message says Lane. The map search selected Road automatically.
Nadia: The organiser must receive a lot of confused calls. There is a special note about the two addresses at the bottom of the invitation.
Peter: Perhaps, but the note only proves that confusion is possible. It doesn't tell us how many people call.
Nadia: Fair correction. Let's check the walking route. We have twenty minutes, and the real centre is only six minutes away. My confidence arrived before my reading skills today.

questions.prompt: What material is the actual door here? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “This door is wooden” — bu eshik yog‘och.

questions.prompt: Which street is the centre on? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Our message says Lane” — College Lane.

questions.prompt: Which inference does Peter challenge: A wrong street or B many confused calls? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: Peter “It doesn't tell us how many people call” deb ikkinchi taxminni cheklaydi.

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada manzil bo‘yicha ikki kuchli taxmin ayting; sherik dalilning kuchini tekshirsin.
success: Must va can't dalilga mos.
Could bilan bitta savol bor.
Bitta ortiqcha qat’iy xulosa yumshatiladi.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda tushlikdagi chalkashlikni hamkasblarga tushuntiruvchi tahliliy paragraf yozing.
writing.model: The twelve extra lunches must belong to the class in the garden. Their teacher brought twelve trays, and the class ordered food this morning. The meals can't simply be unwanted. Our first explanation about a school trip was not supported by the calendar. Could our daily sheet prevent this problem next time? I think it could, with a column for each group's eating location. Numbers alone do not explain where people are. The cook prepared the correct quantity, so we should not describe this as a cooking mistake. The problem was communication between the classroom and the kitchen, and a small change could make that communication clearer.
success: 100–120 so‘z bor.
Must va can't kamida bittadan dalil bilan ishlatilgan.
Muammo va aniq tuzatish ayblovsiz tushuntirilgan.

skills.teacherNote: Oldindan: tray — patnis, column — ustun, laboratory — laboratoriya. Readingda noto‘g‘ri va to‘g‘ri dalilni ajrating; listeningda Peterning tuzatishini ikkinchi tinglashda toping. Sekin o‘quvchiga evidence→deduction qolipi; ilg‘orga kuchli va kuchsiz must misolini baholatish. Scaffold: could not be bu hikoyada o‘tmishdagi imkonsizlik; faol topshiriqda hozirgi can't ishlatiladi.

skills.objective: Hozir davom etayotgan taxmin va o‘tgan voqea taxminini modal shakllar bilan farqlayman.

reading.title: The Warm Printer
reading.text: When I entered the library office at seven, the printer was warm and a stack of certificates lay beside it. Nobody was there. The librarian must have printed them recently, I thought. Yet her coat was missing, and she usually arrives after eight. A volunteer might have come early instead. The computer screen showed a document called Garden Awards, but a filename could have remained open from the previous evening. I noticed a handwritten message: 'Please leave these for the breakfast group.' That explained the purpose, although not the person responsible. Someone might be preparing the ceremony downstairs now. I took the certificates to the kitchen and found the caretaker arranging flowers. He had printed them during his early shift. The machine's warmth had been useful evidence of recent activity, but it had not identified the user. A printer can reveal timing without revealing a name.

questions.prompt: What was beside the printer? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A stack of certificates” — sertifikatlar.

questions.prompt: Who actually printed them? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “He had printed them” oldingi caretakerga ishora.

questions.prompt: What did warmth support: A recent use or B the librarian's identity? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Useful evidence of recent activity” — yaqinda ishlatilganini, kimligini emas.

listening.title: A Closed Workshop
listening.text:
Rafi: The workshop door is locked, but I can hear a machine. They might be cutting wood in the back room.
Ella: They must have changed the entrance arrangements. A new sign points to the side gate.
Rafi: Or they could have locked this door just for the delivery. There is a truck outside.
Ella: True. The message on my phone says the session starts at two. I might have missed an update, though.
Rafi: Let's ring the bell at the side gate. We shouldn't stand here inventing a mystery about a perfectly ordinary door.
Ella: Someone is coming. She may be carrying the materials for our class.
Rafi: Yes, she has a box of safety glasses. The sound must have been a demonstration, not a full lesson. Still, we should ask rather than treat that as certain.
Ella: Agreed. Hearing a machine tells us something is happening, not exactly what.

questions.prompt: Where does the new sign point? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Points to the side gate” — yon darvozaga.

questions.prompt: What is the person carrying? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A box of safety glasses” — himoya ko‘zoynaklari.

questions.prompt: What time does Ella's message give? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The session starts at two” — soat ikkida.

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada printer voqeasiga hozirgi bir taxmin va o‘tmishdagi ikki taxmin ayting; ularning dalilini ko‘rsating.

Must/might have + V3 o‘tmishga tegishli.
Shaxs va vaqtga oid dalillar aralashtirilmagan.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda yopiq ustaxona yonidagi kuzatuvlaringizni ehtiyotkor xulosa bilan yozing.
writing.model: The workshop team might be preparing our materials in the back room. We can hear a machine, and a woman is carrying safety glasses. They may have moved the entrance because a delivery truck is outside the main door. The new sign must have been put there for a reason, but we do not yet know whether the change is permanent. Ella might have missed a message about it. We should ring the side bell and ask where to wait. The sound suggests activity, but it does not prove that our lesson has already started. Checking directly will give us a clearer answer than guessing outside.

reading.title: The Missing Booking
reading.text: Our debate team arrived at the hall and found a yoga class inside. We had booked the space by phone, but nobody had sent written confirmation. The manager checked the system: our request was still marked 'awaiting details'. We couldn't have completed the booking, because the final form was blank. I had assumed the phone conversation was enough. I should have asked for confirmation, and the office should have explained the final step clearly. We shouldn't have invited an audience before checking the room. Fortunately, the library offered us a smaller space. Some teammates wanted to blame one person, but that would have hidden the shared process problem. After the debate, we created a simple checklist with a named person for each stage. The yoga class kept its calm atmosphere; our team gained a practical lesson about paperwork without needing to practise any difficult poses.

questions.prompt: What was happening in the hall? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A yoga class inside” — yoga darsi.

questions.prompt: Why was the booking incomplete? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Because the final form was blank” — yakuniy shakl bo‘sh.

questions.explanation: “The library offered us a smaller space” — kutubxona.

listening.title: The Deleted Recording
listening.text:
Host: Our interview file is missing. I can't have deleted it this morning; I haven't opened the folder today.
Editor: I moved some files last night. I should have checked the names before moving them.
Host: We shouldn't have used titles like Final, Final New and Really Final. Those names are almost an invitation to confusion.
Editor: I agree. But moving is not deleting. The file could still be in the archive folder.
Host: Here it is, under Tuesday Interview. We should have included the guest's name and the date.
Editor: Let's rename it and make a backup before we edit. I am relieved, but this was avoidable.
Host: So am I. The guest gave us an hour of her time. Losing that would be more serious than losing our tidy desktop.
Editor: I'll write a short naming guide. No file should need to shout 'really final' at its neighbours.

questions.prompt: Who moved files last night? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “I moved some files last night” — muharrir.

questions.prompt: Where was the interview? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “In the archive folder … Here it is” — arxivda.

answers: the guest's name and the date
questions.explanation: “The guest's name and the date” — mehmon ismi va sana.

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada bron xatosini ayblovsiz tahlil qiling: imkonsiz taxmin, qilinishi kerak bo‘lgan ish va qilinmasligi kerak bo‘lgan ish.
success: Can't/couldn't have dalil bilan bog‘langan.
Should have va shouldn't have + V3 bor.
Tuzatish shaxsni ayblashdan ko‘ra jarayonga qaratilgan.

writing.model: We should have named the interview file with the guest's name and the recording date. Titles such as Really Final did not tell us enough. The host can't have deleted the file this morning because she did not open the folder. The editor moved it last night, and it was still safe in the archive. We shouldn't have assumed that a missing file was a deleted file. Before our next interview, we should agree on a naming system and a backup location. One person should check both copies after recording. This will protect the guest's contribution and save the team from another unnecessary search.

reading.title: A Festival without Enough Chairs
reading.text: Our film night attracted more visitors than expected. We could have borrowed chairs from the sports hall, but we decided the thirty seats in our room would be enough. Several people watched from the floor, and one cheerful visitor called it an unusually realistic camping film. The joke helped, but comfort still mattered. Next month, attendance is likely to rise because the local college is sharing our programme. Bad weather is unlikely to reduce numbers much; the event is indoors and close to a bus stop. We will probably need fifty chairs, although we should count registrations before arranging transport. The organiser definitely wants to keep entry free. That makes borrowing more suitable than buying. Our mistake was not a lack of options. We had an option and chose not to use it. A better estimate and an early phone call could prevent a repeat.

questions.explanation: “The thirty seats in our room” — o‘ttizta.

answers: the college is sharing the programme
the local college is sharing their programme
local college is sharing their programme

questions.prompt: What does the organiser definitely want to keep free? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)

listening.title: The Train We Didn't Take
listening.text:
Lena: We could have taken the direct train, but we chose the cheaper bus. Now we are arriving an hour later.
Sam: The delay is frustrating, but the price difference paid for lunch. I don't think the decision was completely unreasonable.
Lena: Fair point. Next time, the early train is likely to be busy because the exhibition opens at nine.
Sam: We should probably book seats a week ahead. Tickets are unlikely to become cheaper on the day.
Lena: I definitely don't want another journey with three changes.
Sam: Then let's compare the whole journey, not only the fare. A cheap ticket can cost time and energy.
Lena: Agreed. We still have four hours at the exhibition today, so the trip isn't ruined.
Sam: Exactly. We can learn from the choice without turning one late bus into a national transport disaster.

questions.explanation: “The cheaper bus” va narx farqi tushlikka yetgani sababni beradi.

questions.prompt: How long do they still have at the exhibition? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada kino kechasi uchun o‘tgan imkon va keyingi safar ehtimolini bog‘lab tavsiya bering.
success: Could have + V3 bajarilmagan imkonni bildiradi.
Likely/unlikely to dan bittasi ishlatiladi.

I definitely support keeping entry free. We should therefore ask the sports hall about borrowing chairs before considering a purchase. One volunteer can count bookings while another arranges collection. This approach uses evidence, protects our small budget and gives visitors a more comfortable evening.

reading.title: The Unclaimed Exhibition
reading.text: Three framed photographs arrived at our youth centre without a sender's note. They showed the old railway bridge, so they might belong to the local history group. However, the group's organiser denied sending them. A delivery label carried yesterday's date, which meant the parcel couldn't have been waiting in our office for weeks. We should have recorded the driver's details, but reception had been busy. The frames were new, and someone must have spent money preparing the pictures. That made throwing them into storage a poor response. We posted a neutral description online without publishing the photographs. By evening, a former member contacted us. She had intended them for next month's exhibition but had forgotten the note. We could have guessed correctly, yet a careful enquiry worked better. Clear labels are likely to become a firm rule for future donations, alongside a rather less official request for readable handwriting.

questions.explanation: “Showed the old railway bridge” — eski temiryo‘l ko‘prigi.

questions.prompt: Who sent them? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A former member contacted us … She had intended them” — sobiq a’zo.

questions.prompt: What ruled out weeks in storage? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A delivery label carried yesterday's date” — kechagi sana.

listening.title: The Quiet Ticket App
listening.text:
Manager: Online bookings have dropped, but the theatre may not be losing interest. The ticket app might be failing.
Analyst: The phone bookings are normal. That supports your idea. We should have tested the update before releasing it.
Manager: Could customers be giving up at the payment screen?
Analyst: Possibly. I tried twice, and both payments failed. The app can't be working reliably.
Manager: We could have kept the old version available, but we removed it too soon.
Analyst: The technician is checking it now. She is likely to find the problem today, though I can't promise a time.
Manager: Then we will probably direct customers to phone booking temporarily.
Analyst: Yes, and explain why. Silence may look like indifference. Customers should not need detective skills just to buy a seat for a comedy.
Manager: I'll prepare a brief notice with the phone number and an apology.

Bitta taxminning chegarasi aytiladi.

reading.title: Why the Seed Tray Fails
reading.text: Our gardening group keeps a notebook of repeated problems. If seedlings get too little light, they grow long and weak. If we water them too heavily, the soil stays wet and the roots struggle. These statements describe regular patterns, not one future experiment. Last month, we moved half the trays to a brighter window and kept the other half on the original shelf. The brighter group grew shorter, stronger stems. However, light was not the only difference: the window area was also cooler. We therefore avoid claiming that our small comparison proves everything. What happens if we change two conditions at once? We cannot easily identify the cause of an improvement. Our next trial will change only the location of the lamp. The notebook has become more valuable than our enthusiastic guesses. Even the tray labelled 'Guaranteed Success' now carries a question mark, which is probably its most scientific feature.

questions.prompt: What happens with too little light? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “They grow long and weak” — bo‘yi cho‘zilib zaiflashadi.

questions.explanation: “The window area was also cooler” — harorat.

questions.explanation: “Only the location of the lamp” — faqat bitta omil.

listening.title: The Shared Calendar
listening.text:
Trainer: What happens if two people edit the same event without checking each other?
Assistant: We sometimes get conflicting times. If the organiser doesn't name an owner, everyone assumes somebody else will check it.
Trainer: Exactly. If an event has one named owner, questions reach the right person. That doesn't mean nobody else can help.
Assistant: Our volunteers worry that ownership means extra work.
Trainer: It usually means a clear point of contact. If the owner is away, a deputy takes over. We write both names on the calendar.
Assistant: And if the time changes?
Trainer: The owner updates the calendar and sends a message. If people only change the calendar, some participants miss the news.
Assistant: So the system needs a record and a notification.
Trainer: Yes. A perfect calendar is not useful if nobody knows it has changed. Our old one was accurate in the same way a secret is accurate: quietly, and for very few people.

questions.prompt: How many names go on the calendar? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Both names” — mas’ul va o‘rinbosar.

questions.prompt: Who takes over when the owner is away? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A deputy takes over” — o‘rinbosar.

questions.prompt: What must accompany a calendar update? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Updates the calendar and sends a message” — xabar ham kerak.

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada ko‘chat tajribasini tushuntiring: uch takroriy sabab–natija va bitta tekshirish savoli.
success: Uch if + Simple, Simple gapi bor.
Bir inkor shart ishlatiladi.
Bir shart savoli va cheklov tushuntiriladi.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda umumiy kalendarni yuritish qoidalarini sabab–natija bilan yozing.
writing.model: If an event has no named owner, questions often go unanswered. Our calendar should therefore show an organiser and a deputy for every activity. If the organiser is away, the deputy checks messages and updates the details. If a time changes, the responsible person sends a notification as well as editing the calendar. A silent change does not reach people who have already written down the old time. If two volunteers notice conflicting information, they contact the owner before making separate corrections. This system does not prevent teamwork. It makes teamwork clearer by giving everyone a reliable place to ask questions and report problems.
success: 100–120 so‘z bor.
Uch zero conditional ma’noga mos.
Mas’uliyat va xabar berish farqi aniq.

skills.teacherNote: Oldindan: seedling — nihol, deputy — o‘rinbosar, notification — bildirishnoma. Readingda sabab va natijani ulang; listeningni ikki bor o‘qib jarayonni chizing. Sekin o‘quvchiga if/then jadvali; ilg‘orga ikki omilli tajribaning cheklovini ayttiring.

skills.objective: First conditional yordamida real kelajak rejasi va inkor natijani ifodalayman.

reading.title: A Rain Plan for the Street Fair
reading.text: The street fair committee has finally written a rain plan. If the forecast shows heavy rain on Friday, we will move Saturday's book stalls into the school hall. Food sellers will stay under the covered entrance because cooking is not allowed indoors. If the hall is unavailable, we won't cancel immediately; we will ask the sports centre about its smaller rooms. Some traders dislike changing locations because customers may miss them. The committee will print a simple map if a move becomes necessary. Will volunteers be able to guide visitors if the weather turns suddenly? Two teams have agreed to stand at the original entrances. The plan costs a little extra, but it protects a month of preparation. Nobody can promise sunshine. The chairperson says her official responsibility ends at arranging shelter, not negotiating directly with the clouds. Everyone accepts that reasonable limit on her otherwise ambitious job description.

questions.prompt: When is the fair? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Saturday's book stalls” — yarmarka shanba.

questions.prompt: Where will food sellers remain? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Stay under the covered entrance” — yopiq kirish ostida.

questions.prompt: What will help customers find relocated stalls? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Print a simple map” — xarita.

listening.title: The Trial Evening Class
listening.text:
Tutor: If twelve people register by Monday, we'll open the evening class next month.
Learner: Will you run it if only ten people join?
Tutor: We won't decide on numbers alone. If a partner organisation covers the room fee, ten may be enough.
Learner: Some parents can't arrive before seven.
Tutor: If the group prefers a later start, we'll discuss seven thirty with the caretaker. We won't promise that time until the building confirms it.
Learner: That sounds fair. Will there be online materials if somebody misses a lesson?
Tutor: Yes. If a learner is absent, we'll send the tasks, but they will still need to practise with a partner later.
Learner: So flexibility doesn't mean doing nothing.
Tutor: Exactly. An evening course should fit real lives without turning into a collection of unread attachments. Our first job is to find a schedule people can actually keep.

questions.prompt: What is the normal registration target? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “If twelve people register” — o‘n ikki.

questions.prompt: Who must confirm a later start? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Until the building confirms it” va caretaker bilan kelishish — bino mas’ullari.

questions.prompt: What must absent learners do later? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Practise with a partner later” — juftlik mashqi.

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada yomg‘ir rejasini himoya qiling; sherik ikki if savolini bersin.
success: Ikki real kelajak sharti bor.
Will/won't natijasi to‘g‘ri.
Bir yes/no shart savoliga javob bor.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda ochiladigan kechki kurs shartlarini izchil tushuntiring.
writing.model: If twelve learners register by Monday, the centre will open an evening course next month. If only ten register, the team will look for help with the room fee before making a final decision. We won't announce a later starting time until the caretaker confirms access to the building. If parents prefer seven thirty, their request will be part of that discussion. Absent learners will receive the lesson tasks, but they will also need partner practice. This arrangement offers flexibility without removing responsibility. A useful course needs both a realistic timetable and regular participation, so registration numbers should not be the only consideration.
success: 100–120 so‘z yozilgan.
Kamida uch real shart/natija bor.
Tasdiqlanmagan vaqt va qatnashish mas’uliyati ajratilgan.

skills.objective: Unless, wh-shart savoli va modal/buyruq natijalari bilan ko‘rsatma beraman.

reading.title: The Repair Voucher
reading.text: Our neighbourhood repair scheme gives residents a voucher for one basic assessment. Unless you book a time, the mechanic cannot guarantee a same-day check. If you arrive early, wait in the marked area rather than beside the workbench. What should you do if the repair costs more than the voucher covers? Ask for a written estimate before agreeing. Some residents thought the voucher promised a complete free repair, so the organisers changed the information leaflet. The new version explains the difference between assessment and repair in large print. If a part is unavailable, you can take the item home and return later. You do not have to leave it indefinitely. The scheme aims to reduce waste, but it must also respect people's time and budgets. A free assessment is useful only if its limits are clear. Small print should not be the most physically demanding part of fixing a chair.

questions.prompt: What does the voucher cover? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “One basic assessment” — dastlabki ko‘rik.

questions.prompt: What should residents request before extra costs? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Ask for a written estimate” — yozma narx hisoboti.

questions.prompt: Must an item stay if a part is unavailable? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “You can take the item home” — olib ketish mumkin.

listening.title: A Safe Route Home
listening.text:
Coordinator: What will your group do if the main path floods?
Walker: We'll use the higher path by the school.
Coordinator: Good. Unless the weather improves, don't cross the stream. If you are unsure, call the group leader.
Walker: Can we split into smaller teams if some people walk slowly?
Coordinator: Yes, if each team has an experienced adult and a phone. Keep everyone informed before separating.
Walker: What if a phone has no signal?
Coordinator: Stay together and return to the last marked junction. Don't invent a shortcut. The route card gives the landmarks in order.
Walker: So speed is not our main target.
Coordinator: Exactly. Finishing safely matters more than finishing early. We can change the plan if conditions change, but we shouldn't change it secretly. A group walk is not a competition to discover how many different directions ten people can choose.

questions.prompt: Which backup path will they use? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
answers: the higher path by the school
questions.explanation: “The higher path by the school” — maktab yonidagi baland yo‘l.

questions.prompt: What must each smaller team have besides a phone? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “An experienced adult and a phone” — tajribali katta kishi.

questions.prompt: Where should they return without signal? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Return to the last marked junction” — oxirgi belgilangan chorrahaga.

speaking.prompt: 90 soniyada ta’mirlash taloni shartlarini tushuntiring, what if savoliga maslahat bering.
success: Unless ma’nosi inkor shartiga mos.
If bilan modal va buyruq natijasi bor.
Bir ehtimoliy vaziyatga aniq javob bor.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda sayr guruhi uchun tushunarli xavfsiz yo‘l ko‘rsatmasini yozing.
writing.model: If the main path floods, use the higher route beside the school. Unless the weather improves, do not cross the stream. Call the leader if you are unsure about the conditions. You can divide into smaller teams if each team has an experienced adult and a working phone. Tell the other team before separating. What should you do if there is no signal? Stay together and return to the last marked junction. The route card lists landmarks in order, so keep it accessible. Our aim is a safe shared walk. Arriving early is not a success if part of the group is missing.
success: 100–120 so‘z bor.
Unless va ikki if ko‘rsatmasi aniq.
Shartlar manbadagi xavfsiz tartibni saqlaydi.

skills.teacherNote: Oldindan: voucher — talon, estimate — taxminiy hisob, junction — yo‘llar tutashuvi. Readingda bepul xizmat chegarasini belgilang; dialogni ikki bor o‘qib qaror daraxtini yarating. Sekin o‘quvchiga unless=if not tayanchi; ilg‘orga noaniq ko‘rsatmani aniqlashtirish.

skills.objective: Second conditional bilan hozirgi noreal taklif va uning oqibatini baholayman.

reading.title: If the Square Had No Cars
reading.text: Our youth council is discussing an imaginary car-free square. If the town removed parking from the centre, there would be space for trees, benches and a small performance area. Some students see only benefits. A shopkeeper is less certain: if customers could not park nearby, they might shop elsewhere. Another resident argues that people would stay longer if the square felt pleasant. Neither claim is a fact yet. We would need information about deliveries, disabled access and current shopping habits before supporting a permanent change. Would residents accept a trial if it lasted only one Sunday? Several local businesses say they would. That seems more useful than designing an expensive fountain immediately. If we spent the entire budget on a beautiful feature, we wouldn't have money to test practical access. Our dream square needs imagination, but it also needs a way for someone to deliver a crate of tomatoes.

questions.prompt: What concern does the shopkeeper raise? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “They might shop elsewhere” — mijozlar boshqa joyga ketishi.

questions.prompt: How long is the proposed trial? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Only one Sunday” — bir yakshanba.

questions.prompt: What could use the entire budget? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “An expensive fountain” va “entire budget” — favvora.

listening.title: The Four-Day Club
listening.text:
Chair: Would you support a four-day working week for our community office if the hours were longer?
Volunteer: I would consider it, but I wouldn't support closing on our busiest day. People need help on Fridays.
Chair: If we moved the quiet Wednesday hours to other days, we could keep Friday open.
Volunteer: That would suit some staff. However, if parents worked longer evenings, childcare might become harder.
Chair: True. We would need individual schedules, not one rule for everyone.
Volunteer: Would the public understand the new timetable?
Chair: They would if we explained it clearly and kept the phone line open.
Volunteer: Then I would support a short trial, not an immediate permanent change.
Chair: Agreed. A calendar with fewer workdays is attractive, but it does not automatically create fewer responsibilities. The office plants will still expect somebody to remember them.

questions.prompt: Which day must remain open? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “People need help on Fridays” — juma.

questions.prompt: What difficulty might longer evenings create? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Childcare might become harder” — bola parvarishi.

writing.model: If our town removed parking from the square, residents would gain space for trees and seating. People might spend more time there, which could help nearby shops. However, some customers would find access harder if they could not park close to the entrances. I would support a one-day trial before a permanent decision. We would need to protect deliveries and disabled access during that trial. If we spent the budget on a fountain first, we wouldn't learn whether the basic plan worked. A modest experiment would give us evidence about movement, shopping and comfort. Attractive drawings alone would not answer those practical questions.

reading.title: A Small Grant, a Large Dream
reading.text: Our reading club can apply for a small grant this month. If we receive it, we will buy portable lights for evening events. That is a realistic plan with a clear price. Our chair also enjoys a bigger dream: if we owned the empty shop next door, we would open a permanent reading cafe. We do not own it, and the grant would not cover a building. Mixing these two ideas in one application could confuse the funder. What would we do if unlimited money were available? That is an interesting planning question, but it is not this application's question. I told the chair, 'If I were you, I would keep the cafe as a long-term ambition and explain the lights first.' She agreed. A modest request is not a lack of vision. It shows that we understand the next useful step. Even a grand library needs somebody to pay attention to the light switch.

listening.title: Choosing a Training Course
listening.text:
Aisha: If I get a place on the local course, I'll study after work. The deadline is Friday.
Ben: What would you do if you could study anywhere?
Aisha: I'd choose a full-time design course abroad, but I can't leave my job now.
Ben: If I were you, I would compare the local course with your actual weekly schedule.
Aisha: I have. If the classes finish at eight, I can catch the last direct bus.
Ben: And if they finished at ten?
Aisha: I would need a taxi, which would make the course too expensive.
Ben: Then transport is part of the decision, not a small detail.
Aisha: Exactly. My dream course is useful for understanding my interests. The real course needs to fit my budget and journey home.
Ben: Sensible. Ambition is excellent, but it should not strand you at a bus stop every Tuesday.

questions.explanation: “The deadline is Friday” — juma.

If I were you bilan asosli maslahat bor.
Savolga vaqt/xarajat dalili bilan javob beriladi.

If the club owned the neighbouring shop, it could create a reading cafe, but that situation is only a dream at present. If I were the chair, I would explain the lighting project first and mention the cafe only as a future ambition. The funder needs to understand what this particular money will achieve. A focused application does not reduce the club's vision. It connects that vision to a practical next step with a realistic cost and an immediate benefit.

reading.title: A Tool Library Proposal
reading.text: Our street association wants a tool library. If people share rarely used equipment, they save storage space and avoid buying the same things repeatedly. That general benefit sounds convincing, but borrowing needs rules. If the pilot opens next month, members will book tools through a simple paper register. Unless a volunteer checks an item on return, damage may go unnoticed. One resident imagines a digital system with automatic lockers. If we had a larger budget, that would be attractive, but we currently have enough money only for shelves and basic repairs. The proposal therefore begins with twenty donated tools and two opening evenings a week. Would more residents join if collection were available on Saturday? The committee will ask before fixing the schedule. A useful service must match people's lives. There is little point in sharing a drill if its opening hours require everyone to become an expert in rearranging their working week.

questions.prompt: Why are automatic lockers not the current plan? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Enough money only for shelves and basic repairs” — mablag‘ cheklangan.

listening.title: The Shared Lunch Decision
listening.text:
Facilitator: If people bring dishes without labels, guests with allergies cannot choose safely. That is our first rule: label ingredients.
Member: If everyone agrees, we'll hold the lunch next Thursday. What will we do if it rains?
Facilitator: We'll use the downstairs room. Unless the lift is working, we won't use the upper floor.
Member: Good. If we had a professional kitchen, we could cook together, but our room only has a kettle.
Facilitator: Then food should arrive ready to eat. If I were you, I would choose something simple to transport.
Member: Would you include neighbours outside the association?
Facilitator: Yes, if we had enough places. For this pilot, we'll reserve ten seats for them and review attendance afterwards.
Member: That balances welcome and capacity.
Facilitator: Exactly. A community lunch needs generosity, but it also needs enough chairs and accurate information about the mysterious green sauce.

questions.explanation: “Label ingredients” — tarkib.

If we had more money, automatic lockers would offer flexible collection, but they are not our first priority. We should ask residents whether Saturday opening would help them. reading.title: The Poster with No Address
reading.text: Our free repair event had tools, volunteers and a cheerful poster. Unfortunately, the poster gave the date but not the address. We shared it online on Wednesday and waited for a busy Saturday. Only regular visitors came. If we had included the address, new residents would have found us more easily. If one person had checked the poster as an outsider, the omission would probably have been obvious. We had all worked in the centre for years, so its location felt like common knowledge. The mistake was not a lack of enthusiasm; it was an assumption about our audience. After the event, we asked two newcomers to review our next announcement. They also wanted bus information and a contact number. If we hadn't made the first mistake, we might not have noticed these wider needs. That does not make the mistake desirable, but it gives the disappointing afternoon a useful consequence.

questions.explanation: “Only regular visitors came” — odatiy tashrifchilar.

answers: bus information and a contact number
bus details and a phone number
transport information and a phone number

listening.title: The Late Team Entry
listening.text:
Captain: If we had submitted our entry on Thursday, we would have met the deadline. I left it until Friday evening.
Member: And if I hadn't assumed you were handling payment, I would have checked it myself. We both missed a step.
Captain: The form was ready, but the payment link closed at five. I thought it stayed open until midnight.
Member: The rules stated five clearly. We should separate the deadline from the day in our checklist.
Captain: Agreed. If our reminder had included the time, we wouldn't have arrived at a closed page.
Member: We can still volunteer at the tournament. That won't replace competing, but we can learn how the event runs.
Captain: Let's do that. I don't want our whole month to become a story about one button we didn't press.
Member: Then next time, one person submits and another confirms. Trust is useful; a receipt is useful too.

If we hadn't asked newcomers to review the next announcement, we might have missed their need for bus details and a phone number too. Our future review should therefore include someone outside the organising team. A checklist can cover date, time, location, transport and contact information. The quiet event was disappointing, but blaming the designer alone would not improve our process. The whole team approved the poster, so the whole team should support the correction.

reading.title: The Interview We Almost Cancelled
reading.text: A local historian agreed to speak at our youth club, but her train was cancelled. We nearly abandoned the session. Instead, one volunteer suggested a phone interview through a speaker. Would we have tried that if our audience had already arrived? Probably not; the extra hour gave us time to test the sound. What might have happened if we had cancelled immediately? Some visitors might have lost interest in future events, although we cannot know that for certain. The remote format had disadvantages: questions were slower, and the historian could not show her maps clearly. However, we recorded the audio with her permission and later added photographs of the maps. If we had insisted on a perfect live event, we could have missed a useful alternative. The result was not identical to our original plan. It was a different event with different strengths, including a historian speaking from her kitchen beside an occasionally opinionated kettle.

listening.text:
Curator: Would we have attracted more visitors if we had used the station hall?
Artist: We might have, because more people pass through it. But many would have been rushing for trains.
Curator: What could we have done to encourage them to stop?
Artist: We could have displayed fewer pieces with larger labels. Our detailed notes suited the quiet library better.
Curator: So the station wasn't automatically a better choice.
Artist: Exactly. If we had wanted brief encounters, it might have worked well. We wanted visitors to spend time with the stories.
Curator: The library gave us that, though attendance was smaller.
Artist: Next time, we could use a small station display to invite people to the main exhibition.
Curator: A combination rather than a competition between venues.
Artist: Yes. The best room depends on the experience we want, not just the number of shoes passing the doorway.

reading.title: The Skill That Opened a Door
reading.text: Two years ago, I joined a free spreadsheet course because a friend needed company. Today, I manage bookings for a community sports centre. If I hadn't taken that course, I wouldn't feel confident with the booking system now. The connection is clear: an old decision supports a present skill. Another connection works in the opposite direction. I am naturally comfortable speaking to strangers. If I were less confident with people, I wouldn't have volunteered to explain the new system at last month's meeting. Neither statement means my career was inevitable. Other people helped, and I still make mistakes. Last week, I briefly booked a room for a meeting of zero people, which was at least easy to organise. Looking back helps me identify useful habits, not write a heroic story about myself. A small opportunity can matter later, especially when we keep practising the skill after the original course ends.

listening.title: The Bike and the Missed Bus
listening.text:
Zara: If I had repaired my bicycle last weekend, I wouldn't be waiting for this bus now.
Imran: Would you be cycling today if the weather were worse?
Zara: Probably not. But the weather is fine, and my tyre is still flat.
Imran: I understand. If I were better at planning, I would have bought my train ticket before the cheap seats disappeared yesterday.
Zara: So your present habit affected a past choice, while my past delay affects this morning.
Imran: Exactly. Neither of us needs a lecture; we need one practical change.
Zara: I'll book the repair today rather than promise to become a completely different person.
Imran: And I'll set a ticket reminder. I am good at remembering concerts but apparently less talented at remembering how to reach them.
Zara: Small systems might help more than dramatic regrets. For now, at least the bus is finally coming.

reading.title: The Courtyard at Midnight
reading.text: Our apartment courtyard is popular in summer, but late conversations echo between the walls. I wish the benches were farther from the bedrooms. That describes a present situation I cannot easily change. I also wish I had raised the problem politely at the residents' meeting last month. Instead, I posted an angry message at midnight, and the discussion became personal. Several neighbours replied that they had nowhere else to meet after work. Their need is real, even if the noise is difficult for others. I wish everyone would lower their voices after ten, and I wish our group chat would stop turning every request into a battle. We are now discussing a quiet period and a different seating arrangement. If only I had begun with those practical suggestions. A complaint can express a genuine problem while still using an unhelpful method. The courtyard needs both conversation and sleep, not a winner.

listening.title: The Group Project Regret
listening.text:
Maya: I wish we had divided the project earlier. Now three people are editing the same section.
Leon: I wish our shared document had clearer headings. I can't tell which comments are still relevant.
Maya: And I wish Dan would reply to messages before changing the slides. His ideas are good, but the timing creates confusion.
Leon: Let's avoid making him the entire problem. I changed two charts without telling anyone yesterday.
Maya: You're right. If only we had agreed on a review process at the start.
Leon: We can still assign sections today and freeze changes an hour before the presentation.
Maya: Good. I wish we had more time, but another complaint won't create it.
Leon: Exactly. Let's make the remaining time useful. Our slides don't need six people moving the same comma around like an expensive piece of furniture.

reading.title: The Accessible Garden Visit
reading.text: Our class is planning a garden visit with several older neighbours. One resident said, 'I wish I could walk the whole route, but my knee makes that difficult.' The organiser replied that shorter routes were available. We hope the weather stays dry, but we will bring portable seats even if the forecast is good. Comfort should not depend on luck. The garden manager allows us to use the sheltered terrace provided we leave it clean. Volunteers can borrow wheelchairs as long as they return them before closing time. These conditions are practical, not signs of reluctance to welcome us. A student first suggested cancelling the longer walk for everyone. However, residents preferred a choice of routes and a shared tea break afterwards. Inclusion does not always mean doing exactly the same activity. It can mean giving people enough information and support to choose. Our plan now has more options and fewer assumptions about what others need.

Singer: Understood. I wish I had a better microphone too.
Technician: The room includes one. Technique matters more than buying everything immediately.
Singer: That's reassuring. I hope we get a clean recording, but I know it may take several attempts.
Technician: Exactly. A first session is also practice. You don't need to turn every small mistake into proof that you can't sing.
Singer: Good. My notebook has room for notes, not a dramatic resignation speech.

reading.title: A Walk with Too Many Steps
reading.text: Our local history walk attracted thirty residents, but the route included a staircase we had overlooked. Two visitors could not continue. If we had checked access with a wheelchair user beforehand, we would have noticed the problem. I wish we had asked people about their needs instead of assuming that a short distance was automatically easy. If our information sheet were clearer, visitors would have known about the steps before registering. The guide changed the route and brought the group back together at the market, but some trust was lost. We now hope the next walk will rebuild it. A volunteer offered to test alternative routes as long as the team shared the full plan early. We accepted. The aim is not to advertise a perfect service after one correction. It is to show that feedback changes decisions. A route is not accessible merely because an enthusiastic organiser can walk it quickly.

reading.title: Where the Cups Go
reading.text: At our community cafe, reusable cups are collected at a separate counter. Staff check each cup, and damaged ones are removed from service. The remaining cups are washed, dried and stored upside down. This process sounds simple, but customers often leave cups in the paper recycling bin. A sign saying 'Staff collect cups here' was replaced with 'Cups are collected here', beside a large arrow. The new wording puts the object in focus, which helps people looking for somewhere to return it. However, grammar alone cannot fix poor placement. The first sign stood behind a plant, where it was almost invisible. We moved it to eye level and watched what happened over three busy afternoons. Incorrect returns fell noticeably. We cannot separate the effect of wording from the effect of position, but together the changes helped. The plant still has a place in the cafe; it no longer manages customer information.

listening.title: A Day at the Repair Hub
listening.text:
Presenter: What happens to a donated bicycle when it arrives here?
Mechanic: Every bicycle is labelled with a number. Its brakes and tyres are checked before anybody rides it.
Presenter: Who decides what needs replacing?
Mechanic: A trained volunteer does the assessment. Useful parts are kept, and worn parts are replaced. We record the work on a card.
Presenter: So the bicycle's history stays with it.
Mechanic: Exactly. The card is given to the new owner. People deserve to know what has been checked, not just hear that the bike looks shiny.
Presenter: Does the system slow you down?
Mechanic: A little at first. But clear records save repeated checks and questions later. Speed is not the only measure of useful work.
Presenter: Your cards sound less exciting than the bicycles, but equally important.
Mechanic: They are. A bell makes noise; a record makes responsibility visible.

reading.title: A Bench with a Second Life
reading.text: The long bench outside our library was made from an old classroom door. A local carpenter built it during last summer's repair festival. Today, it is used by readers, bus passengers and people who simply need a rest. Is the bench treated with a special coating? Yes, it is protected against rain. It is not painted every month; volunteers inspect the surface and refresh the coating when necessary. Where is similar furniture made? The workshop behind the library produces small items from donated wood. The project is not presented as a solution to all waste. Some materials are unsafe or too damaged to reuse. Still, the bench offers a visible example of a useful second life. A small label tells its history. Several former pupils enjoy sitting on it, perhaps because it is the first classroom door that has ever encouraged them to stay outside for longer.

listening.title: The Local Soap Stall
listening.text:
Customer: Is this soap made here in town?
Seller: Yes. It is produced in a small workshop near the river. The business was started by two sisters three years ago.
Customer: Is it tested on animals?
Seller: No, it isn't. The supplier documents are available on our website. You should check those details rather than rely only on a friendly face at a stall.
Customer: I appreciate that. Is the wrapping recyclable?
Seller: The paper is, but the small label is not accepted by our local collection service. We are looking for an alternative.
Customer: So the packaging isn't completely recyclable yet.

reading.title: The Newsletter That Never Arrived
reading.text: Our residents' newsletter was not delivered to three buildings last week. At first, the editor assumed the volunteers had forgotten them. Was the route map checked before delivery? Yes, it was, and all three buildings appeared on it. Were enough copies printed? The printer's record confirmed that they were. The real problem was at the entrance: new security codes had not reached the delivery team. Copies were left at the management office instead, but no notice explained where residents could collect them. The team had completed part of the task without completing the communication. We changed the checklist to include access details and a fallback message. The editor also apologised for the early accusation. A missing newsletter does not automatically prove a careless volunteer. Asking precise questions about each stage produced a fairer explanation than turning the delivery bag upside down and hoping responsibility would fall out with the spare copies.

reading.title: The Square's Trial Weekend
reading.text: The town square will be closed to private cars for one trial weekend next month. reading.title: The Repair Shop Window
reading.text: When I visited the repair shop on Tuesday, an old radio was being examined on the main bench. Two chairs were being sanded near the window. I asked whether the radio could be repaired economically. The technician explained that a replacement part might cost more than a similar second-hand radio. Could the original case be kept while the inside was replaced? Technically, yes, but the owner valued its original sound as well as its appearance. The decision was therefore not only financial. While we talked, the owner arrived with a photograph of his father using the radio. That did not make every repair price reasonable, but it explained why a simple cost comparison was incomplete. The technician offered a written estimate and two options. Good repair advice should make choices clearer, not decide how much another person's memory is worth. The radio remained silent, but the conversation around it was unusually informative.

questions.prompt: What was being examined? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “An old radio was being examined” — radio.

questions.prompt: How many chairs were being sanded? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Two chairs” — ikkita.

questions.prompt: What did the owner bring? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A photograph of his father using the radio” — otasi surati.

listening.title: The Event Setup Review
listening.text:
Organiser: Could the stage be moved closer to the wall next time?
Technician: Possibly. When I arrived yesterday, it was being assembled in the middle because the wall sockets were being checked.
Organiser: Could the cables be covered more securely?
Technician: Yes. Extra covers can be hired. The team was being shown the cable route when the first musicians arrived, which interrupted the briefing.
Organiser: So an earlier setup would help.
Technician: It would, but we also need a clear handover. People shouldn't guess which checks are complete.
Organiser: Can the final inspection be recorded on one sheet?
Technician: Certainly. Name the person responsible for each item and leave space for unresolved issues.
Organiser: That sounds more useful than simply writing 'all fine'.
Technician: Exactly. A check sheet should describe reality, not offer the room an encouraging compliment before the audience walks in.

questions.prompt: Why was the stage in the middle? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
answers: the wall sockets were being checked
questions.explanation: “Because the wall sockets were being checked” — rozetkalar tekshiruvi.

questions.prompt: What interrupted the briefing? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The first musicians arrived” — musiqachilar kelishi.

questions.prompt: What can record the final inspection? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Recorded on one sheet” — bitta tekshiruv varag‘i.

speaking.prompt: Ikki daqiqada radio ta’miri variantlarini so‘rang; tashrif paytidagi ikki jarayonni tasvirlang.
success: Ikki Can/Could … be V3 savoli bor.
Was/were being + V3 bilan ikki jarayon bor.
Narxdan tashqari bir mezon asoslangan.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda sahna o‘rnatish jarayoni bo‘yicha tavsiya yozing.
writing.model: When the technician arrived, the stage was being assembled away from the wall because the sockets were being checked. The cable route was being explained when musicians interrupted the briefing. Could setup begin earlier next time? That would help, but timing alone would not solve every problem. Extra cable covers can be hired, and the final inspection can be recorded on one sheet. Each item should name the responsible person and show any unresolved issue. A general statement that everything is fine gives little useful information. A clear handover would help the next team understand what has been checked and what still needs attention before the audience arrives.

skills.objective: Past Continuous Passive inkor/savoli va Past Perfect Passive bilan oldin tugagan ishni ajrataman.

reading.title: The Hall before the Meeting
reading.text: When the residents arrived, the hall was not being cleaned as the booking email had suggested. Cleaning had been completed at noon, and the chairs had been arranged before three. The room was locked because a missing key had caused a delay. Was the entrance being repaired? No; a contractor was working on the office door farther along the corridor. Several people connected the visible tools with the locked hall and assumed the wrong cause. The organiser eventually found the spare key in a labelled cabinet. Afterwards, we compared the booking message with the actual sequence of events. It described an activity that was no longer happening and omitted the person responsible for opening the room. We changed the handover note to show completed tasks, current work and the key holder separately. A useful update should explain time as well as activity. Otherwise, yesterday's instruction can become today's very convincing misunderstanding.

questions.prompt: When had cleaning been completed? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Completed at noon” — tush payti.

questions.prompt: Why was the hall locked? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “A missing key had caused a delay” — kalit yo‘q edi.

questions.prompt: Which door was actually being worked on? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The office door farther along the corridor” — idora eshigi.

listening.title: The Packing Room Check
listening.text:
Supervisor: Was the order being packed when you arrived at nine?
Assistant: No, it wasn't being packed then. The boxes had been sealed before my shift started.
Supervisor: Had the labels been printed too?
Assistant: Yes. They had been placed beside the boxes, but nobody had attached them.
Supervisor: So the order was not ready for collection.
Assistant: Correct. The driver was waiting, and I initially thought the labels on the desk belonged to another order.
Supervisor: Was the packing area being used by another team?
Assistant: No. The confusion came from the status note. It said 'packed', which sounded complete.
Supervisor: We need separate stages for sealed, labelled and ready to collect.
Assistant: Agreed. One short word was doing three jobs badly. A little more detail would have saved the driver from a long discussion with a pile of anonymous boxes.

questions.prompt: What time did the assistant arrive? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “At nine” — to‘qqizda.

questions.prompt: What had been done to the boxes? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The boxes had been sealed” — yopib muhrlangan.

questions.prompt: What had not yet been attached? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Nobody had attached them” — yorliqlar.

speaking.prompt: Ikki daqiqada zal tayyorligi haqidagi chalkashlikni vaqt ketma-ketligida izohlang.
success: Bir was/were being savoli va inkori bor.
Had been + V3 bilan oldingi ish berilgan.
Ko‘rinadigan dalil va asl sabab farqlangan.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda buyurtma holatini qayd etish uchun tahliliy tavsiya yozing.
writing.model: The order was not being packed when the assistant arrived at nine. The boxes had been sealed before the shift began, and the labels had been printed. However, the labels were still on the desk, so the order was not ready for collection. The status word packed hid that unfinished step. We should use separate labels for sealed, labelled and ready to collect. A final check should connect each box with its delivery information. This change would give both staff and drivers a clearer picture of progress. Short updates are useful only when their meaning is shared. Otherwise, saving a few words can create a much longer delay.
success: 100–120 so‘z yozilgan.
Past Perfect va davomiy passiv farqlangan.
Jarayonning uch bosqichi va asos bor.

skills.teacherNote: Oldindan: contractor — pudratchi, seal — muhrlab yopmoq, status — holat. Readingda vaqt jadvalini chizing; dialogni ikki bor o‘qib completed/unfinishedni belgilang. Sekin o‘quvchiga before/when tayanchi; ilg‘orga qisqa, ammo aniq holat nomlarini yaratish.

skills.objective: Past Perfect Passive savol/inkori va by orqali oldingi ish hamda bajaruvchini aniqlayman.

reading.title: The Exhibition Credit
reading.text: A photograph in our exhibition carried the wrong photographer's name. The image had been donated by a family member, but the original creator had not been identified before printing. Had the donation form been checked? Yes, although the form named the donor rather than the photographer. Those roles had been treated as identical. A visitor recognised the picture and contacted the actual photographer, who was disappointed but willing to help correct the record. The label was replaced, and an explanation was added to the exhibition page. We did not simply remove the mistake quietly. The photographer wanted the correction to be visible because credit was part of the work's history. Our new form separates creator, donor and rights contact. It takes longer to complete, but the extra distinctions matter. A name beneath a picture is not decorative furniture. It tells readers whose effort they are seeing and whose permission may be needed.

questions.prompt: Who donated the image? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Donated by a family member” — oila a’zosi.

questions.prompt: Whose name did the form actually identify? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Named the donor rather than the photographer” — hadya qiluvchi.

questions.prompt: Why was a visible correction wanted? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
answers: credit was part of the work's history
questions.explanation: “Credit was part of the work's history” — mualliflik tarixi uchun.

listening.title: The Group Tickets
listening.text:
Leader: Had our seats been reserved before the payment deadline?
Agent: The request had been entered by your colleague, but the seats hadn't been confirmed. Payment was still missing.
Leader: I thought the email was a confirmation.
Agent: It was an acknowledgement of the request. The subject line was not clear enough, and I understand the confusion.
Leader: Had a reminder been sent?
Agent: Yes, but it went to the address on the form. Your colleague says that mailbox is no longer checked.
Leader: Then both our details and your wording need attention.
Agent: Agreed. I can offer another departure with enough seats, but it leaves an hour later.
Leader: Please hold it while I contact the group.
Agent: I will send a message explicitly marked 'held, not paid'. We should not make a booking depend on interpreting polite but ambiguous language.

questions.prompt: Who entered the request? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Entered by your colleague” — rahbarning hamkasbi.

questions.prompt: Why hadn't seats been confirmed? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Payment was still missing” — to‘lov yo‘q.

questions.prompt: How much later is the alternative? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “An hour later” — bir soat.

speaking.prompt: Ikki daqiqada surat muallifligi tekshiruvini qayta qurib ayting va bajaruvchilarni by bilan aniqlang.
success: Had … been savoli bor.
Hadn't been + V3 to‘g‘ri.
By bilan donor va muallif farqi saqlanadi.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda surat yorlig‘i xatosidan keyingi tuzatish tamoyilini yozing.
writing.model: The photographer had not been identified before the exhibition label was printed. The donation form had been checked, but it named the donor, not the creator. A family member had supplied the image, and the team incorrectly treated that person as its photographer. The correction should therefore be visible rather than quietly replacing one name with another. Credit forms part of the picture's history. Our new form should distinguish creator, donor and permission contact. Each role answers a different question. This will add work at the beginning, but it will reduce confusion later and show respect for the people whose images make the exhibition possible.

Ikki Past Perfect Passive va bir inkor bor.

skills.objective: 21-haftadagi kengaytirilgan passiv shakllarni loyiha tekshiruvida birlashtiraman.

reading.title: The Reopening Report
reading.text: The swimming pool will be reopened only after the final inspection. New filters have already been fitted, and damaged tiles were being replaced when the residents' committee visited on Tuesday. The changing rooms were not being used during that work. Had the emergency signs been checked before the visit? The manager showed a signed record confirming that they had. However, the accessible entrance had not been tested by users with mobility needs. The committee recommended a practical visit rather than relying only on measurements. Small difficulties can be missed on a drawing. The manager agreed that the route could be assessed by a local access group before opening. The report therefore records substantial progress without calling the pool ready. Some residents want a firm date, which is understandable after a long closure. Still, a date should follow completed checks rather than pressure staff to describe unfinished work as complete. A reopened door is useful only when people can actually get through it.

questions.prompt: What was being replaced on Tuesday? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Damaged tiles were being replaced” — shikastlangan plitkalar.

questions.prompt: Which entrance had not been user-tested? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The accessible entrance had not been tested” — qulay kirish.

questions.prompt: Who could assess the route? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “By a local access group” — qulaylik guruhi.

listening.title: The Festival Equipment Audit
listening.text:
Auditor: Will the borrowed speakers be returned tomorrow?
Organiser: Yes. They must be checked before transport. One cable was being repaired when I left the workshop.
Auditor: Had the equipment list been updated before collection?
Organiser: Most of it had, but the extra microphone hadn't been added. It was supplied by the school at the last minute.
Auditor: Can that be corrected now?
Organiser: Yes. The microphone is here, and the school has confirmed its number.
Auditor: Good. The return record should show each item and its condition. Was anything being used during the final count?
Organiser: No. Everything was on the table, though two cases were closed.
Auditor: Then open them and check the contents. An empty case can look impressively complete from outside.
Organiser: Agreed. We need evidence of the equipment, not just a tidy photograph of its luggage.

Measurements are useful, yet they may miss practical difficulties. A firm opening date will be welcomed by residents, but it should follow evidence rather than replace it. reading.title: Two Accounts of One Meeting
reading.text: After the residents' meeting, two summaries appeared in our group chat. One said the caretaker was against the new garden. The other said he supported it. I had taken notes, so I checked his actual words. He said he liked the idea but did not have time to water the beds every evening. He told the committee he could help with repairs at weekends. His objection concerned responsibility, not the garden itself. Both summaries had removed the condition that made his position understandable. I posted a fuller account and asked the writers to correct their messages. Neither had intended to mislead anyone; each had remembered the part that matched an existing opinion. Reporting speech is therefore more than changing pronouns and verbs. It requires selecting fairly. Our final minutes recorded support for the garden and a request for a separate watering team. A useful summary should shorten a discussion without shrinking the people in it into convenient labels.

questions.prompt: What task did the caretaker lack time for? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Did not have time to water … every evening” — kechki sug‘orish.

questions.prompt: What help did he offer? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Help with repairs at weekends” — dam olish kunlari ta’mir.

questions.prompt: Was he against the garden itself? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “His objection concerned responsibility, not the garden” — loyiha emas, vazifa masalasi.

listening.title: The Customer's Actual Complaint
listening.text:
Assistant: The customer said the whole workshop was useless.
Manager: Did she use those words?
Assistant: Not exactly. She said she didn't understand the online instructions. She told me the practical demonstration was helpful.
Manager: Then we should keep both points. Otherwise, we might change the wrong part of the service.
Assistant: She also said she wanted more time to practise before the final task.
Manager: That's a specific request. Did she say the tutor was unhelpful?
Assistant: No. She said he answered questions clearly, but the group was too large.
Manager: Good. Write that accurately. We need feedback we can act on, not a dramatic headline.
Assistant: I see the difference. My summary turned several useful comments into one negative judgement.
Manager: It happens easily. Listening fairly means preserving the parts that complicate our first impression, even when a shorter story would fit neatly into the message box.

questions.prompt: Which instructions were unclear? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Didn't understand the online instructions” — onlayn yo‘riqnoma.

questions.prompt: What part was helpful? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The practical demonstration was helpful” — amaliy ko‘rsatish.

questions.prompt: What group issue did she identify? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “The group was too large” — guruh kattaligi.

speaking.prompt: Ikki daqiqada qarovchining pozitsiyasini ikki gap bilan adolatli yetkazing, noto‘g‘ri xulosani tuzating.
success: Said va told + object to‘g‘ri.
Ko‘chirma inkor va tasdiq bor.
Pozitsiyaning muhim sharti yo‘qolmagan.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda mijozning fikrini rahbar uchun xolis paragrafga aylantiring.
writing.model: The customer said she did not understand the online instructions, but she told the assistant that the practical demonstration was helpful. She also said she wanted more time to practise before the final task. Her comments did not describe the whole workshop as useless. She praised the tutor's clear answers while pointing out that the group was too large. A fair summary should preserve this mixed view. The centre could review the written instructions, allow extra practice and consider group size. Changing the practical demonstration would not address the concern she actually raised. Accurate reporting helps the team improve the right part of the service rather than react to an exaggerated headline.

reading.title: The Promise in the Interview
reading.text: On Monday, the organiser told our student reporter, 'We are preparing a free skills fair. We have contacted local employers, and we will publish the programme on Friday.' The reporter's draft said the organiser was preparing the fair, had contacted employers and would publish the programme on Friday. Those changes preserved the timing of the interview. However, the draft also said every employer would offer a job. That promise had never been made. The organiser had said employers could explain training routes, not guarantee employment. We corrected the article before publication and kept a short quotation beside the summary. The exercise showed that accurate grammar does not automatically produce accurate journalism. A sentence can have perfect backshift and still report an invented commitment. Our editor now asks two questions: does the language match the original time, and does the claim match what was actually said? Both checks matter more than making the event sound impressive.

questions.prompt: When would the programme be published? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Will publish … Friday” — juma.

questions.prompt: What had organisers contacted? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Have contacted local employers” — mahalliy ish beruvchilar.

questions.prompt: What had not been promised? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Not guarantee employment” — kafolatli ish va’da qilinmagan.

listening.title: Passing on the Engineer's Update
listening.text:
Supervisor: What did the engineer tell you yesterday?
Assistant: She said she was checking the damaged pump. She said she had ordered a replacement part and could return on Thursday.
Supervisor: Did she promise the system would work that day?
Assistant: No. She said she would test it after fitting the part, but she couldn't guarantee the result before that test.
Supervisor: Good. Our notice must not turn an expected visit into a confirmed reopening.
Assistant: I wrote that the engineer had ordered the part and would return for further work. Is that clear enough?
Supervisor: Add that testing is still required. Residents need to understand the remaining condition.
Assistant: Understood. The original update was careful, but it would be easy to make it sound more certain while shortening it.
Supervisor: Exactly. A summary should remove extra words, not remove the uncertainty that keeps the message honest.

questions.prompt: What had been ordered? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Had ordered a replacement part” — ehtiyot qism.

questions.prompt: When could the engineer return? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Could return on Thursday” — payshanba.

questions.prompt: What is still required before reopening? (Qisqa javobni inglizcha yozing.)
questions.explanation: “Testing is still required” — sinov.

speaking.prompt: Ikki daqiqada intervyuni ertasi kuni xabar sifatida yetkazing, va’da bilan imkonni ajrating.
success: Present→past va perfect→past perfect to‘g‘ri.
Will→would hamda can→could misoli bor.
Kafolatlanmagan natija kafolat sifatida berilmagan.

writing.prompt: 100–120 so‘zda muhandisning kechagi xabarini aholiga xolis yetkazing.
writing.model: The engineer said she was checking the damaged pump and had ordered a replacement part. She told the team she could return on Thursday. She did not promise that the system would reopen that day. Instead, she said she would test it after the part was fitted and could not guarantee the result before testing. Our public notice should preserve that condition. An expected visit is evidence of progress, but it is not a confirmed completion date. The team should publish another update after the test. This wording may sound less exciting than a reopening announcement, yet it gives residents a more accurate basis for planning.
